Relative-importance networks with the psychnets R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/relative-importance-networks.Rmd
relative-importance-networks.Rmd

How much of a model’s explanatory power can be attributed to each predictor when the predictors overlap? In psychological and educational questionnaires, self-efficacy, motivation, learning strategies and self-regulation may explain some of the same variation in an outcome. Multiple regression coefficients describe each predictor’s adjusted association, but do not allocate the variance explained jointly by several predictors. Relative importance analysis instead partitions the model’s R2R^2 among predictors, including their shared contributions. Approaches to this problem include dominance analysis (Budescu, 1993) and other relative importance indices (Johnson & LeBreton, 2004). The LMG decomposition (Lindeman et al., 1980; Groemping, 2006) calculates each predictor’s average increase in R2R^2 over all possible orders in which predictors can enter the model.

Psychological networks offer a complementary way to study relationships among measured constructs. Rather than designating a single outcome in advance, a network represents variables as nodes and their relationships as edges. In education, network approaches have been used to examine complex learning processes and the relations among psychological constructs (Saqr et al., 2024). Studies of self-regulated learning have investigated the dynamics of regulation during academic writing (Saqr et al., 2021) and the association between students’ monitoring events and phases of regulation (Malmberg et al., 2022). These applications illustrate the value of examining a system of related learning processes rather than interpreting each construct in isolation. However, an edge in a conventional partial correlation network represents a conditional association, not a share of explained variance.

A relative-importance network combines the network representation with an explained-variance decomposition. Each construct is treated in turn as the outcome of a regression on all the other constructs. The LMG shares become directed edges: an edge from A to B gives the proportion of B’s total variance attributed to A within that regression. The incoming edges sum to B’s R2R^2, whereas outgoing edges summarise how much A contributes across the other outcomes. This direction indicates which variable is the predictor and which is the outcome; it does not imply a causal effect. Relative-importance networks are therefore useful when the research aim is to compare explanatory contributions among correlated constructs, rather than to estimate direct conditional associations or causal pathways.

This article demonstrates the approach with five self-regulated learning constructs using the psychnets package. It introduces the LMG decomposition, fits and interprets a directed network, verifies that the incoming shares sum to each construct’s explained variance, and distinguishes predictability from outgoing contribution. It then compares Pearson-based results with a network based on Spearman rank correlations and outlines reporting and interpretation considerations. The example uses language-model-generated questionnaire responses, so its numerical findings illustrate the method rather than provide evidence about students.

library(psychnets)

The model

For each outcome jj, the other nodes form the predictor set PP. The LMG share of predictor kk is its average incremental contribution to R2R^2 over all possible orders of predictor entry. Equivalently, it averages the change in R2R^2 when kk is added to a subset SS of the remaining predictors, with weights that give each ordering equal importance:

φkj=∑S⊆P\{k}|S|!(|P|−|S|−1)!|P|![R2(S∪{k})−R2(S)]. \varphi_{kj} = \sum_{S \subseteq P \setminus \{k\}} \frac{|S|!\,(|P| - |S| - 1)!}{|P|!} \left[R^2(S \cup \{k\}) - R^2(S)\right].

Each R2(A)R^2(A) follows from the correlation matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S} as R2(A)=𝐒jA𝐒AA−1𝐒AjR^2(A) = \mathbf{S}_{jA}\mathbf{S}_{AA}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{Aj}. The shares are non-negative and add up to the outcome’s full-model explained variance,

∑kφkj=Rj2. \sum_{k} \varphi_{kj} = R_j^2 .

The edge from kk to jj has weight φkj\varphi_{kj}. Its value is a share of the outcome’s total variance, not a fraction of the explained variance alone. Incoming weights sum to the outcome’s R2R^2, while outgoing weights sum the predictor’s contributions across the other outcomes. These totals have different interpretations and should not be compared as though they measured the same property. For pp nodes, each outcome involves 2p−12^{p-1} predictor subsets. Computation therefore becomes increasingly demanding as the network grows, and the default limit is 21 nodes.

Data

SRL_GPT contains 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, represented by five construct scores on scales from 1 to 7. These responses were generated by a large language model (GPT) for a study of how language models answer psychological surveys (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). They provide an illustrative dataset with related constructs, not observations of students. Accordingly, the results below should not be interpreted as findings about student behaviour or learning.

  • Nodes: five construct scores, treated as continuous: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value), SE (self-efficacy), SR (self-regulation) and TA (test anxiety). Each is in turn the outcome of a linear regression and a predictor in the four others.
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
head(SRL_GPT)
#>        CSU       IV       SE       SR   TA
#> 1 5.307692 5.666667 5.777778 5.333333 4.00
#> 2 5.846154 6.444444 6.000000 5.777778 4.00
#> 3 6.615385 6.666667 6.222222 6.333333 3.25
#> 4 5.692308 6.555556 6.333333 5.555556 4.50
#> 5 4.384615 5.555556 4.888889 4.777778 4.00
#> 6 4.846154 5.444444 5.666667 5.111111 3.50

How is each construct’s explained variance divided?

psychnet() with method = "relimp" estimates a relative-importance network by treating each of the five constructs in turn as an outcome and decomposing its regression R2R^2 among the other four constructs.

importance_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "relimp")
summary(importance_net)
#> <psychnet> relimp network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 20   (directed)
#>   structural certificate (decomposition residual): 2.22e-16
#>   edge weight: range [0.006, 0.299], mean 0.165

The fitted network contains 20 directed edges, one for each ordered pair of distinct constructs. All estimated shares are positive, ranging from 0.006 to 0.299 when rounded to three decimal places. In the edge table, from identifies the predictor and to identifies the outcome:

as.data.frame(importance_net)
#>    from  to      weight
#> 1    IV CSU 0.288505266
#> 2    SE CSU 0.263574096
#> 3    SR CSU 0.274082666
#> 4    TA CSU 0.007326148
#> 5   CSU  IV 0.299473895
#> 6    SE  IV 0.216286692
#> 7    SR  IV 0.258608009
#> 8    TA  IV 0.007032583
#> 9   CSU  SE 0.280588934
#> 10   IV  SE 0.219009605
#> 11   SR  SE 0.220573037
#> 12   TA  SE 0.006045547
#> 13  CSU  SR 0.277393999
#> 14   IV  SR 0.253052645
#> 15   SE  SR 0.212824511
#> 16   TA  SR 0.052422918
#> 17  CSU  TA 0.014154964
#> 18   IV  TA 0.015416846
#> 19   SE  TA 0.012055817
#> 20   SR  TA 0.127772080

The largest edge runs from cognitive strategy use to intrinsic value (0.299). This means that cognitive strategy use is allocated approximately 29.9% of the total variance in intrinsic value, within the regression containing all four other constructs. The reverse edge, from intrinsic value to cognitive strategy use, has weight 0.289. Although these values are similar, they refer to different outcomes and need not be equal. Among cognitive strategy use, intrinsic value, self-efficacy and self-regulation, the directed shares range from 0.213 to 0.299. All three other learning constructs therefore make appreciable contributions to each of these outcomes.

The pattern differs for test anxiety. Self-regulation has an incoming share of 0.128 for test anxiety, compared with 0.014 for cognitive strategy use, 0.015 for intrinsic value and 0.012 for self-efficacy. In the reverse direction, test anxiety contributes between 0.006 and 0.007 to the explained variance of cognitive strategy use, intrinsic value and self-efficacy, and 0.052 to that of self-regulation. Thus, self-regulation has the largest relative-importance link with test anxiety in both directions. These shares do not establish that self-regulation mediates the relations between test anxiety and the other learning constructs.

Do the shares add up to each construct’s explained variance?

An important check is whether the incoming shares reproduce the R2R^2 of each full regression. certificate() reports the largest absolute difference between these quantities across the five nodes. A value near zero indicates that the estimated weights satisfy the decomposition identity to numerical precision.

certificate(importance_net)
#>   method  certificate       kind certified
#> 1 relimp 2.220446e-16 structural      TRUE

The reported discrepancy is 2.220446×10−162.220446 \times 10^{-16}, below 10−1510^{-15} and consistent with numerical rounding. The edge weights thus reproduce each outcome’s explained variance to machine precision. This is a check of the decomposition, not evidence that the regressions meet their assumptions or fit the data adequately.

How much of each construct is explained?

net_predict() gives the R2R^2 for each construct when predicted by all four others. This is also the sum of that construct’s incoming raw relative-importance shares.

net_predict(importance_net)
#>   node     type metric predictability accuracy
#> 1  CSU gaussian     R2      0.8334882       NA
#> 2   IV gaussian     R2      0.7814012       NA
#> 3   SE gaussian     R2      0.7262171       NA
#> 4   SR gaussian     R2      0.7956941       NA
#> 5   TA gaussian     R2      0.1693997       NA

The four predictors jointly account for approximately 83% of the variance in cognitive strategy use (R2=0.833R^2 = 0.833), 80% in self-regulation (R2=0.796R^2 = 0.796), 78% in intrinsic value (R2=0.781R^2 = 0.781) and 73% in self-efficacy (R2=0.726R^2 = 0.726). Predictability is substantially lower for test anxiety (R2=0.169R^2 = 0.169): the other constructs explain approximately 17% of its variance. Self-regulation’s share of 0.128 represents about three quarters of this explained variance, with most of test anxiety’s total variance remaining unexplained by the model.

Which constructs contribute most to explaining the others?

net_centralities() reports each node’s outgoing strength, the sum of its contributions to the regressions for the other constructs. Since every edge weight is non-negative, strength and expected influence are identical for this network.

net_centralities(importance_net)
#>   node  strength expected_influence
#> 1  CSU 0.8716118          0.8716118
#> 2   IV 0.7759844          0.7759844
#> 3   SE 0.7047411          0.7047411
#> 4   SR 0.8810358          0.8810358
#> 5   TA 0.0728272          0.0728272

Self-regulation has the highest outgoing strength (0.881), followed closely by cognitive strategy use (0.872). Test anxiety has the lowest (0.073). Self-regulation’s leading total reflects its contributions to the other learning constructs as well as its comparatively large share in test anxiety. Outgoing strength summarises how much a construct contributes to explaining the other outcomes across separate regressions. It should be reported separately from incoming R2R^2, which describes how well the construct itself is explained.

What does the network look like?

cograph::splot() displays the network with arrows indicating the predictor-to-outcome direction and edge labels showing the raw LMG shares.

cograph::splot(importance_net, directed = TRUE, edge_labels = TRUE)

Because the network contains all 20 possible directed edges, the plot is relatively dense. The larger reciprocal shares among the four learning constructs contrast with the generally smaller links involving test anxiety. The edge table is preferable when precise numerical comparisons are needed.

Do the conclusions depend on the correlation estimator?

As a sensitivity analysis, the network can be re-estimated using Spearman correlations with cor_method = "spearman". This substitutes rank-based associations for Pearson correlations in the decomposition; it does not change the variables or the number of nodes.

importance_spearman <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "relimp",
                                cor_method = "spearman")
as.data.frame(importance_spearman)
#>    from  to      weight
#> 1    IV CSU 0.286725129
#> 2    SE CSU 0.270159694
#> 3    SR CSU 0.265419989
#> 4    TA CSU 0.005393971
#> 5   CSU  IV 0.299066051
#> 6    SE  IV 0.203370231
#> 7    SR  IV 0.263749828
#> 8    TA  IV 0.005279123
#> 9   CSU  SE 0.292490014
#> 10   IV  SE 0.206036816
#> 11   SR  SE 0.209495026
#> 12   TA  SE 0.004346020
#> 13  CSU  SR 0.271471270
#> 14   IV  SR 0.260383389
#> 15   SE  SR 0.203334385
#> 16   TA  SR 0.037126693
#> 17  CSU  TA 0.009240756
#> 18   IV  TA 0.011339759
#> 19   SE  TA 0.008842802
#> 20   SR  TA 0.086215285
net_predict(importance_spearman)
#>   node     type metric predictability accuracy
#> 1  CSU gaussian     R2      0.8276988       NA
#> 2   IV gaussian     R2      0.7714652       NA
#> 3   SE gaussian     R2      0.7123679       NA
#> 4   SR gaussian     R2      0.7723157       NA
#> 5   TA gaussian     R2      0.1156386       NA

The largest directed share is again from cognitive strategy use to intrinsic value (0.299). For the four learning constructs, rank-based R2R^2 values range from 0.712 to 0.828, compared with 0.726 to 0.833 in the Pearson-based network. Test anxiety shows a more noticeable difference: its R2R^2 decreases from 0.169 to 0.116, while self-regulation’s share in that outcome decreases from 0.128 to 0.086. The broad pattern of larger shares among the learning constructs is similar under both estimators, but the strength of the explained-variance links involving test anxiety is sensitive to the correlation method.

Reporting the analysis

When reporting a relative-importance network, researchers should specify the constructs, sample size, correlation estimator, handling of missing values, and whether the displayed edge weights are raw or normalised. Edge directions should be defined as predictor to outcome, with weights interpreted on the appropriate variance scale. Incoming R2R^2 and outgoing strength answer distinct questions and should be presented separately. Sensitivity analyses can help readers assess how strongly conclusions depend on the chosen correlation estimator.

For example, this analysis used raw LMG shares based on Pearson correlations from 300 complete sets of language-model-generated responses. The network contained 20 directed edges, of which the largest connected cognitive strategy use to intrinsic value (0.299). Node predictability ranged from R2=0.169R^2 = 0.169 for test anxiety to R2=0.833R^2 = 0.833 for cognitive strategy use. Self-regulation accounted for 0.128 of test anxiety’s total variance, the largest incoming share for that outcome. Under Spearman correlations, the learning constructs retained broadly similar patterns, whereas test anxiety’s R2R^2 fell to 0.116.

Assumptions and when to use relative importance

  • Each outcome is modelled through a regression on the remaining nodes. Interpretation therefore depends on the suitability of the regression and correlation assumptions, including linear relationships and independence of observations.
  • Relative importance partitions explained variance among correlated predictors. It does not estimate unique conditional associations. When those associations are the research focus, a partial correlation network, such as one estimated with the graphical lasso, is more suitable.
  • Raw weights retain the outcome’s variance scale: a share of 0.1 represents one tenth of its total variance. normalized = TRUE instead rescales each outcome’s incoming shares to sum to one. Such weights compare the relative allocation within an outcome but no longer show how much variance the predictors collectively explain.
  • Edge direction identifies the predictor and outcome in a regression. It does not establish temporal order, causal influence or mediation.
  • The number of predictor subsets doubles with each additional node. This makes the method most practical for small or moderate networks.
